manuscript_title: Molecular and Structural Characterization Reveals Divergent Extracellular Vesicle Profiles Between Wild Type and Alzheimer's Disease Cerebrocortical Organoids

required_revisions.text: Add 2–3 fully independent, interleaved differentiation batches per genotype for the EV proteomics comparison, process them blind, and report the number of biological replicates; aggregate statistical analysis to the organoid/batch level (the number of batches, not the number of injections), and re-report the differential protein lists (170/184) and all fold-changes/p-values on this basis. If this is not feasible, explicitly demote the differential-proteomics and EV-count claims from findings to candidate observations.

Add the decisive controls to the co-culture experiment to establish that the Aco-650 signal in WT organoids is vesicle-mediated transfer rather than free-dye diffusion or soluble-factor effects: (a) an EV-depleted AD conditioned-medium control added to a naive WT organoid, (b) a transwell insert that allows soluble factors but blocks vesicles, and (c) a dye-only (no-organoid) washout control showing the dye is fully removed post-rinse. Report the Aco-650 concentration in the medium at day 0/1/4/7.

Reconcile the abstract with the body text: remove or qualify 'wider size distribution' (contradicted by the authors' own 'not significantly different' and by vFC showing identical medians) and 'differential expression of tetraspanins CD63, CD9, CD81' (contradicted by 'phenotypically similar' and TS at/below the LOD). Scale the 'non-cell-autonomous spread of amyloid-containing EVs' claim to 'transfer of endosomal material and amyloid-associated signal,' explicitly flagging the templating interpretation as unproven.

For the co-culture Aβ quantification, state the number of independent organoids per condition, report the Arivis 'Simple Threshold' value used, and re-analyze with organoid as the independent unit (e.g., mixed-effects model or aggregation to organoid level) rather than treating images as the experimental unit.

Quantify the frequency of multilamellar vesicles and fibril-containing vesicles per genotype from the cryo-TEM data (report total micrographs per genotype, not just 'positive' ones), and either molecularly identify the fibrillar material (immunogold or targeted proteomics) or explicitly state that its identity is unconfirmed.

Deposit the cryo-EM movies/micrographs in an accessible repository (EMPIAR accession) and state the classification criteria for 'fibril' vs artifact; state the final volume of the concentrated EV sample after the 10K MWCO spin column and the overall concentration factor from the 120 mL conditioned media so the reported EV concentrations can be reproduced.

Add a statement in Methods or Acknowledgements covering (a) informed consent/IRB approval for the original donor-derived hiPSC derivation and (b) that the present reuse/EV study falls within the scope of that consent or an IRB 'not human subjects research' determination by the receiving institution, citing the relevant protocol/MTA identifier.

Add biological negative controls for the ThT/AmyTracker signal (e.g., EVs from a non-AD or non-neuronal source, and RNase A/proteinase K digest controls to exclude RNA or non-amyloid hydrophobic aggregates), and report the n and error bars for the ThT assay.

minor_suggestions: Add a positive control (an EV preparation known to express CD63/CD9/CD81) to the tetraspanin immunoprecipitation workflow to exclude the null that the capture did not work, particularly for the tau-negative result.
Normalize EV counts and concentrations to organoid number, mass, or cell count so the 2x EV difference can be attributed to the mutation rather than culture size.
Pin the GitHub analysis code with a commit hash or archived DOI, and deposit the custom Python scripts used for the cryo-TEM violin plots.
Complete the reference list entries that lack volume/page identifiers (e.g., Fowler 2025, Mao 2025, Forero 2024) and confirm the Jakhria 2014 attribution for the membrane-rupture claim.
Acknowledge the contradicting Halipi 2024 finding (EVs slow Aβ aggregation) in the sentence claiming EVs enhance aggregation propensity.
Define the arrow colors in the Figure 4 legend and state what the Aco-650 signal represents in the Figure 7 WT-organoid image.

weaknesses.text: **Load-bearing claim 1 — human-derived cells used without an ethics/consent statement.** The entire study rests on hiPSC lines "derived from a male donor" (Section 2.1), obtained from the Tessier-Lavigne laboratory and the New York Stem Cell Foundation. No sentence states (a) the original derivation received informed consent / IRB approval of the donor, or (b) the present laboratory use was reviewed. Under the standard that silence is not compliance, the absence of any statement is a hard finding, not a shrug. The plain alternative explanation for the omission — the donors were consented at the NYSCF and the current work falls under standard cell-line reuse — may be true, but the reader cannot verify it, and the manuscript as written is not, on its face, in compliance. The one thing that would settle it: a statement in Methods or Acknowledgements explicitly noting informed consent for donor-sourced lines, naming the derivation body and giving evidence of the receiving site classification of this reuse. It is a one-paragraph amendment but a required one.

**Load-bearing claim — continuous scope of secondary use.** The organoid EV work goes beyond the original cell-line derivation: the cells are being used in organoid and a related protocol the donor likely never encountered, and the manuscript gives no material-transfer or biobank statement covering the ISCI lines. If the original repository consent is restricted, the research is conducted and the claimed de-identification and evidence disappears. The alternative (the original consent is broad or the reuse is covered by the NYSCF Material Distribution Agreement, which is common) also exists. A line must specify that the requisite scope of reuse is covered; before that, the entire model rests on the provenance of the cells. The change: confirm for the existing repository that the cell lines' use is in agreement with the MTA and donor; the word "male donor" is not anonymity for personal data — and this sentence gives a λεγmen.

questions: What is the explicit sentence at Methods (or its same level) that covers (a) the original donor consent for the hiPSC derivation and (b) that the current reuse/EV study falls under the scope of that consent or an IRB "not human subjects research" determination by the receiving institution?

Doyou have the protocol or MTA identifier from Tessier-Lavigne/NYSCF that documents the applicable informed-consent limits? (A simple citation to that protocol would resolve both of my stated claims.)

weaknesses.text: Pseudo-replication in the co-culture experiment. The claim that WT organoids co-cultured with AD organoids accumulate more intratissue Aβ (Figure 7C–D) rests on a Student's t-test over "n = 27 images for WT+AD and n = 49 images for WT+WT". Images are not the independent unit of analysis. If these images are drawn from one (or even a few) organoids per condition, the effective sample size is the number of organoids, not the number of images, and the p-value — whatever it is — is meaningless: standard errors are minimized by the number of tiles 27/49, not 2–4. The text never states how many independent organoids were co-cultured per condition, nor whether images were sampled randomly, staged, or selected for quality. A ROSOM with organoid as random effect, or an analysis aggregated to the organoid level, is what the comparison actually requires.

vFC vesicle-count and size claims have no stated test and no independent replication. The report "The AD organoid EV isolate contained more EVs compared to the WT organoid (~3.1 e9/mL vs 1.6 e9/mL)" and the "wider size distribution" advance in the Abstract are not supported by any statistic in the text. Each value appears to come from a single EV isolate per genotype — one pooled 120 mL harvest per apS. That yields * n = 1 per condition, for which no inferential statement is possible. The size/count comparisons are thus descriptive figures, not findings, and should be either accompanied by at least 3–6 biologically independent EV preparations (collections separated in time, and compiled), or explicitly demoted from claims you made to observations. "Very low levels of tetraspanin expression (~20 ABC per EV)" is likewise a single estimate not subject to actual variant measurement.

The "significant" proteomics list has *n* = 1 biological sample per genotype. Deep profiling from a single AST/AD pooled conditioned-media harvest, run in "technical triplicate", produces 3848 proteins with 170 (WT)-upregulated and 184 (AD-upregulated) at FC ≥ 2 / adj p ≤ 0.05 — and a series of strongly errant candidate numbers e.g. RAB8A, FC 2.2, adj p = 0.030. The reported p-values and adj.p-value sequences measure protocol reproducibility between three injections of one biological mixture, not biological signal between genotypes. The multiple-comparison correction (MSstats dataProcess) is performed correctly, but correct science gating cannot rescue biological replication that is not recorded. Every differential-importclaim resting on these lists is over-stated to the precision the design supports; the experience is reframable: these are candidate distinguishing proteins — validate on three or more biological replicates are needed.
ThT binding — "25-fold higher than synthetic liposome control" has no stated n, no error bars, and no test; numerically the signal is integer-level; flat line versus a fiber calibration is missing.
He IP-ELISA "Aβ42 — present at the highest level in the TS+ eluate" has no stated n, no test, no input-size normalization — one trifecta of undefined statistics.

We lower variance in the FT0 bar plot was not defined as "SEM" or "SD"; figure legends don't provide exact p-values, no CIs, at "value > threshold (yet 4.3.2 'n = technical replicates' pre-defines the whole paper's level of replication as technical-ended).

L scalar "elementary instrument-free" image-based quantitative measure (copy the ROUT-detect outputs) — the size of the FDR on repeated-measures that would have been obtained by 4-difference shrinkage — neither the Αβ-threshold or the normalization coefficient (per cell) — for "volume per cell" as reported now established.

The abstract's "differential expression of tetraspanins CD63, CD9, CD81" — is not supported even at the descriptive level of §3.2, which says the populations were "phenotypically similar" and showed "very low TE". This is not a question; it is a direct contradiction.

The fibrillar-material claim rests on cryo-EM micrographs that are not deposited. The central structural finding — AD organoid EVs contain "luminal fiber-like structures" and "fibrils with amyloid-like twists, resembling PHF-type tau" (Figure 4I) — is a visual identification. The micrographs are not deposited in EMPIAR or any accessible repository, and the data availability statement gates "all other data" behind "reasonable request," which is not availability. An independent group cannot verify the fibril identification or distinguish it from membrane fragments or staining artifacts. The fix: deposit the cryo-EM movies/micrographs with an EMPIAR accession and state the classification criteria for "fibril" vs. artifact.

The reported EV concentrations are not reproducible because the final concentration factor is unspecified. The vFC reports "~3.1 e9 EVs/mL in the concentrated media compared to 1.6 e9/mL for the WT" (Figure 3), but the protocol says the 2 mL SEC eluate was concentrated "until the desired volume was reached" — the final volume, and hence the concentration factor from the 120 mL conditioned media, is not given. The reported per-mL concentrations cannot be reproduced or compared back to the original media. The fix: state the final volume and the overall concentration factor.

The co-culture Aβ quantification cannot be rerun without the threshold value and biological n. The Aβ puncta analysis uses "Simple Threshold analysis operator" with no threshold value given, and the n=27 (WT+AD) / n=49 (WT+WT) images are not tied to a stated number of independent organoids per condition. The threshold directly determines the segment volume, so the reported increase in WT+AD cannot be reproduced. The fix: report the threshold value and the number of organoids per condition.
The GitHub analysis code has no commit/tag or archived DOI, so the exact analyzed version is not pinned (SOFT).
The custom Python scripts for the cryo-TEM violin plots are not deposited (SOFT).
I could not verify that the PRIDE accession PXD076102 resolves; the format is correct but the link is unverified.
The ThT assay compares 20 µg of EV protein against 2.5e6 liposomes without matching vesicle number or lipid content — a design-adequacy issue for methodology.
The co-culture transfer claim lacks a transwell or EV-depleted-media control to distinguish EV-mediated transfer from free dye/Aβ in the media — a design-adequacy issue for methodology.

questions: What is the final volume of the concentrated EV sample after the 10K MWCO spin column, and the overall concentration factor from the 120 mL conditioned media?
Are the cryo-EM micrographs deposited (EMPIAR accession)? If not, can they be made available?
What threshold value was used in the Arivis "Simple Threshold" operator, and how many independent organoids contributed to the n=27 and n=49 images?
Does the GitHub repository have a tagged release or commit hash?

weaknesses.text: Load-bearing — HARD: the co-culture/"non-cell-autonomous" claim. The abstract concludes "and there is evidence of endosomal membrane transfer between isogenic cultures with an increase of Aβ peptides in the WT organoids." The design supports the conclusion only if the fluorescent signal that appears in the WT is actually transferred intracon membra — but the Aco-650 stained AD organoid was merely "rinsed several times" and then co-cultured for 7 days. With no evidence that free dye is fully removed from the well, the fluorescent signal observed in the WT could be dye diffused out (from dead/leaky cells), not vesicle-bound, and taken up directly by WT cells. The claim about the Aβ increase in WT is similarly under-separated: soluble factors, inflammatory mediators, and/or cell stress in the shared well are all plausible causes; the design that would separate EV-mediated transfer from release — passaged AD conditioned medium with EVs vs. EV-depleted AD medium vs. a transwell insert — is not present. What would settle it: (1) a condition in which attempt-confirmed 'no-organoid' or filtered stained-AD medium is added to a naive WT organoid; (2) a transwell that allows soluble factors but the vesicles; /3) an added dye-only control to show the washout kinetics. The second issue is sampling: the quantification reports 27 vs 49 images (z-stacks in the tile), but the number of independent co-culture w characters and the treatment of images as the experimental unit are not disclosed. If 27/49 images came, for instance, from one co-culture, the test is pseudo-replication.

Load-bearing — H2: the EV proteomic differences. The comparison WT vs AD EVs is derived from one prep (pooled above one differentiation batch), analyzed in technical triplicate. Technical NMR of the same peptide digest cannot address the covariate of biological variability — the batch effects of the differentiation procedure and genotype are now intertwined. The stated claims (Chapter 5's "significant differences", "secretory autophagy" protein set) need a design where two to three fully independent, interleaved batches per genotype are processed blind, and the "n" of statistical analysis is the number of batches, not the number of injections. Without this, the 170/184 significant proteins cannot be attributed to M146V.

Load-bearing — H3: "fibrillar material" in EVs. The abstract records "AD-deficient EVs display luminal fibrillar material," but the cryo-EM evidence as reported is: fibrillar in vesicle lumen sections, "often nearby vesicles or in dense clumps," and partly co-purified. If it's adjacent/freely-floating tissue, it is not shown to be luminal; and in the absence of immunolabeling (or a cryo-ET tomography plane through the vesicle), fibrillar morphology alone doesn't establish one protein composition. The fact that WT and AD differences are illustrated with 65 AUC-positive micrographs vs 17 WT—without a per-genotype count of total EVs, the proportion with loose fibrils — only one-quarter. Provide a per-vesicle quantitation and a labeled FIBRIL protein element; otherwise, the distinct claim is not evidenced.

The abstract's "differential expression of tetraspanins" is at odds with the body text stating that WT and AD are "phenotypically similar" — an internal inconsistency; one of the two statements should be changed or shown with precise fluorescence quantified.

The "flat / similar" conclusion from the vesicle flow cytometer relies on `TS` events at or below the antibody binding capacity (ABC) LOD — measuring at the instrument's detection floor can only show "≥", not equivalence, so "phenotypically similar" is unjustified.

In the tetraspin IP experiment, there is a negative bead arm (TS−) but no positive single concentration (i.e., an EV preparation known to express CD63/CD9/CD81 processed through the same workflow); without it, a plausible null ("the capture didn't work") is not excluded — particularly for the tau-negative result (tau was in the flow-through).

The ThT "EVNAMS" assay compares only to liposomes rather than to a biochemically matched EVs able whose protein/RNA are digested (RNase A, proteinase K): since ThT binds RNA and other non‑amyloid hydrophobic aggregates, the signal cannot be called "amyloid in EV" without these digest controls per vesicle.

The tissue/confocal "amyloid in WT" quant is described only as "segmented nuclei + Aβ signal" — no descriptions of how WT vs AD cells were distinguished in the same well, or from when cell lines were preshopped, and no blinding of region selection; which matters in the multiple-extracondition.

questions: What is the level of Aco-650 (or free dye) in the culture medium immediately post-rinse and at day 1/4/7 — and how would you distinguish that pooled "dye in solution" from vesicle-bound dye being taken up by the WT?

How many independent co-cultures were performed per condition, and how were cell traces for analysis assigned to WT versus AD organoid identity after clearing/immunostaining (which organoids in the analysis, if the cell Tracker signal was used)?
Of triple MS injections — are these (y) the three same sample, and how many separate differentiations, were evaluated (by genotype) to independently replicate the protein fold changes in Figure 5A?

In the cryo-EM micrographs counted, how many total micrographs (rather than "positive" ones) are present per genotype — and how many micrographs with fibrillar material adjacent to/hiding in vesicles, i.e., inside the vesicle lumen?

weaknesses.text: The 'non-cell-autonomous spread of amyloid' claim outruns the evidence: the co-culture experiment shows (a) the transfer of Aco-650 endosomal label from AD to WT organ acts and (b) increased amyloid signal in co-cultured WT organ acts, but neither establishes spread of pathology — the Aco-650 transfer shows membrane/endosome transfer, not that the transferred material is amyloid-bearing, and the increased signal in WT could reflect uptake of amyloid monomer/oligomer rather than templated aggregation. The claim of 'modeling non-cell-autonomous spread of amyloid-containing EVs' should be scaled to 'transfer of endosomal material and amyloid-associated signal,' with the templating interpretation explicitly flagged as unproven.

The 'divergent EV profiles' claim rests partly on a comparison that may not isolate genotype: quantification of EV count and size distribution is not normalized to cell number or organoid mass, so the 2x difference may reflect more cells or more secretion rather than the mutation itself.

The fibrillar material in AD EVs is not molecularly identified — no immunogold, cryo-ET, or proteomic confirmation identifies it as tau, amyloid, or anything else; molecular identification would strengthen the novel claim.

questions: Were EV counts and concentrations normalized to organoid number, mass, or cell count, and if not, can the 2x EV concentration difference (3.1 vs 1.6 e9/mL) be attributed to the mutation rather than culture size?
Can the luminal fibrils in AD EVs be identified (immunogold or targeted proteomics), and do they co-localize with the transferred Aco-650 signal in co-cultured WT organoids?
What is the biological negative control for the ThT/AmyTracker signal — do EVs from a non-AD or non-neuronal source show comparable binding?

weaknesses.text: HARD — Title/abstract: 'AD organoid-derived EVs have a wider size distribution' is contradicted by the authors' own text: 'they trended towards a wider, though not significantly different, size distribution' (Fig 4H). The abstract states as fact what the Results report as a non-significant trend.

HARD — Abstract: 'After a 1-week co-culture of AD organoids with WT organoids, there is evidence of endosomal membrane transfer between the isogenic cultures with an increase in amyloid-β peptides in the WT organoids.' The Aco-650 signal in WT organoids is not established as transferred endosomes: the dye is a small fluorophore that can be released from the stained AD organoid, diffuse through shared media, and be taken up by the WT organoid independently of any vesicle. The authors' own design (shared well, full media changes) cannot exclude this. The A-beta increase is correlational and not tied to the dye transfer.

HARD — Abstract: 'These observations support the notion that non-cell-autonomous spread of amyloid-containing EVs in human AD brains can be modeled in a cerebral organoid system.' The co-culture experiment never demonstrates that A-beta moved inside EVs; it shows a dye signal and an A-beta increase in the same well. The claim that this models EV-mediated spread is not supported by the evidence presented.

SOFT — 'EVs purified from AD organoid conditioned media have a wider size distribution' (abstract) also conflicts with the vFC data (Fig 3), which reports similar size ranges for WT and AD (~85–270 nm, median 124 nm for both). The wider-distribution claim rests on the cryo-TEM subset (24 vs 65 EVs), a small and possibly biased sample, and is not corroborated by the flow cytometry.

SOFT — The claim that AD EVs 'show differential expression of tetraspanins CD63, CD9, and CD81' (abstract) is not supported by the vFC data, which report TS expression at or below the limit of detection for both genotypes; the differential expression rests on the proteomics (CD9 up in AD), not on the flow cytometry, and the abstract does not distinguish these.

SOFT — The multilamellar-vesicle claim ('AD organoid-derived EVs can have single, double, and even triple membranes') is based on a small cryo-TEM subset (63 AD micrographs positive for vesicles) without quantification of the frequency of multilamellar forms in each genotype; 'can have' is defensible but the implied divergence is not quantified.

SOFT — The fibrillar material in AD EVs is described as 'amyloid-like' and 'resembling PHF-type tau' in the body, but the abstract's 'luminal fibrillar material' is presented without the caveat that its identity is unconfirmed; the authors themselves note immunogold and cryo-ET are needed.
SOFT — The claim that 'EVs can transfer from AD to WT organoids' (section heading) overstates the evidence, which shows dye co-localization and an A-beta increase, not demonstrated vesicle transfer.

questions: Can you report the Aco-650 signal in WT organoids from a control where the dye is added to media without an AD organoid, and from a transwell/separate-well design that prevents direct contact while sharing conditioned media — to distinguish vesicle-mediated transfer from free-dye diffusion?
Can you quantify the frequency of multilamellar vesicles and fibril-containing vesicles per genotype from the cryo-TEM data, rather than presenting representative micrographs?
Can you reconcile the abstract's 'wider size distribution' claim with the vFC data showing similar size ranges for WT and AD, and with the non-significant cryo-TEM trend?

weaknesses.text: The central claim that co-culturing WT with AD organoids transfers endosomal material and increases intratissue A-beta signal in WT is not fully supported by the text: the Aco-650 transfer is shown in a live-cell image (Figure 7B) but the text does not state how the transfer was quantified or whether the Aco-650 signal in WT was distinguished from background or from the WT organoid's own endosomes. The claim that 'Aco-650 signal was present in the WT organoids' is stated without a control showing that the dye does not leak or transfer via media exchange.

The quantitative claim in the Results that AD organoid media contained 'about twice as many EVs' as WT is not tied to a specific number in the text; the vFC data are presented as ranges and medians but the exact EV counts per mL are not given in the main text, making the 'twice as many' claim unverifiable from the text alone.

The statement that 'AD organoid-derived EVs can have single, double, and even triple membranes' (Abstract) is supported by cryo-EM images, but the text does not quantify how many of the 65 AD EVs were multilamellar versus the 24 WT EVs, so the reader cannot judge whether this is a robust difference or a few striking examples.

The proteomics section reports fold-changes and adjusted p-values for several proteins but does not state the number of biological replicates (only technical triplicates are mentioned), so the reader cannot assess whether the statistical comparisons are adequately powered.

The figure legends are incomplete: Figure 4 legend does not define the color of the arrows (blue for multilamellar, red for fibrils is stated in the text but not in the legend), and Figure 7 legend does not define what the Aco-650 signal represents in the WT organoid image.

The term 'amyloid' is used loosely: the ThT and AmyTracker signals are attributed to 'amyloidogenic proteins' but the text does not state which proteins are being detected, and the possibility that ThT binds to RNA or other polymers is acknowledged in the Discussion but not in the Results where the claim is made.

questions: How many biological replicates were used for the proteomics comparison, and were the technical triplicates from a single EV isolation or from multiple isolations?
In the co-culture experiment, was there a control where Aco-650 was added to media without an AD organoid, to rule out dye transfer via media exchange?
What is the exact EV count per mL for WT and AD isolates, and how was the 'twice as many' claim derived from the vFC data?
For the cryo-EM analysis, how many of the 65 AD EVs were multilamellar, and how many of the 24 WT EVs?

weaknesses.text: Load-bearing. The paper's central claim — that co-culturing a WT organoid with an AD organoid transfers endosomal material and "potentially pathogenic amyloid-β peptides," implying EV-mediated non-cell-autonomous spread — is not established by the evidence cited. The Aco-650 transfer (Fig. 7B) shows membrane transfer but not that it is EV-mediated: the dye could transfer via any secreted vesicle, free dye carryover, or direct cell contact, and the authors state only that Aco-650 "intercalates into endosome membranes," not that it is EV-exclusive. The increased Aβ puncta in co-cultured WT organoids (Fig. 7C–D) is correlative; nothing in the cited data distinguishes EV-mediated Aβ transfer from the WT organoid's own upregulated Aβ production in response to diffusible factors, or from the AD organoid's proximity. The one-week co-culture with full media changes every other day does not exclude soluble Aβ or non-EV particles as the vector. The claim in the abstract that these observations "support the notion that non-cell-autonomous spread of amyloid-containing EVs... can be modeled" outruns the evidence: to support it, the authors would need to show the transferred material is inside EVs (e.g., EV-depleted media control, or fluorescent Aβ tracked within Aco-650+ vesicles) and that the WT Aβ increase is causally linked to that transfer rather than to bystander effects.

Sweep. The novelty claim of EV-mediated inter-organoid amyloid spread is asserted without a comparison to directly competing prior work on EV-mediated Aβ propagation (e.g., Sardar Sinha 2018, which is cited but not positioned against the organoid result) — a completeness gap I could not fully resolve because my searches returned no directly competing organoid-EV-transfer study.

The claim that "amyloid fibrils are established to mediate the rupture of membranes" (Jakhria 2014) is cited to a β2-microglobulin study; the attribution is plausible but I could not verify the specific claim from the abstract, so I ask the authors to confirm the source supports the membrane-rupture point.

The claim that "EVs can enhance the aggregation propensity of amyloidogenic proteins" (Mirdha 2024; Budvytyte & Valincius 2023) is presented as established, yet the directly relevant Halipi 2024 (cited elsewhere) reports EVs slow Aβ aggregation — the contradicting finding is not acknowledged in that sentence, which is a fairness issue.

The Mao 2025 citation (autophagic EVs distinct from exosomes) is used to support the AEV framework; I could not verify this reference resolves, and it appears in the reference list without a volume/page — I ask the authors to confirm the citation is complete and real.

The reference list has several entries with garbled or truncated fields from the PDF conversion (e.g., the Forero 2024 entry runs into page numbers, the Fowler 2025 entry lacks volume/pages), which I flag as a hygiene issue rather than evidence the references are fabricated.

The proteomics section cites the MSstats and DIA-NN pipelines appropriately, but the claim that specific autophagy markers (RAB8A/B, STX3, LC3A/B) constitute "a novel extracellular biomarker signature" is a novelty claim resting on the proteomics interpretation, which the citation record alone cannot support — I attribute this to the novelty reviewer.

questions: Can the authors confirm that the Aco-650 dye is EV-exclusive and does not transfer via free dye or non-EV carriers, and can they report an EV-depleted media control for the co-culture transfer?
Can the authors confirm that Jakhria 2014 (β2-microglobulin) is the correct source for the claim that amyloid fibrils rupture membranes, and that Mao 2025 is a complete, resolvable citation?
Is the increased Aβ signal in co-cultured WT organoids attributable to transferred Aβ rather than to the WT organoid's own upregulated production, and what control would distinguish these?
